## 3. On A Perfect Movie

**Score:** 157
**Body:** Often times, a movie is just a movie. You just move on after spending some of your “free” time with it. On very rare occasions, a movie won’t let you move. It forces you to immerse yourself in another world, to sit for a while and contemplate. The movie ended, the credits are rolling … you’re still sitting there, dazed … 

Usually, it won’t be difficult to find some flaws, or at least some aspects which one thinks could’ve been better. A character which feels like a character, a monologue which is a bit flat, a plot which seems ridden with holes, cinematography which is a bit lacking, etc. But on those rarest of times, you come across a movie so complete that you’re just forced to stand up and salute upon its ending. A great movie is that which makes you forget it’s a movie. The characters so real, the plot so engaging, the dialogues so lively, the cinematography so immersive, … That’s Memories of Murder. 

I shelved it in the row with the best of Scorsese, Tarkovsky, PT Anderson, and Wes Anderson.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Watching Emilia Pérez in 2026 was... a choice

**Score:** 12
**Body:** Let me start by saying that Jacques Audiard is a filmmaker I respected enormously; "A Prophet" is one of my favorite movies of the century; and "Dheepan" is a beautiful refugee drama.

I say this to explain why I finally watched the unhinged musical "Emilia Pérez" after successfully avoiding it two Oscar seasons ago: I didn't follow the award circuit closely and never imagined Audiard was the name behind the film that got tons of Oscar nominations plus an entire country against it.

It wasn’t until yesterday, when "Emilia Perez" popped up on my screen, that I realized Audiard had directed it. So I pressed play, ready to prove the haters wrong.  Well, of course they were right, and now I can see why Mexican viewers had such strong objections.

**Audiard’s genre-blending mess of a movie displays cultural carelessness at best and inhumanity at worst.** I got the impression that Audiard, as a filmmaker, thought he was creating a fantastical version of the country of Mexico, but this isn’t Oz. His dramatic material draws on the real suffering of real people whose lives he didn’t bother to understand.

The more I think about the plot, the more absurd Audiard’s decision to build an original movie musical around cartel violence and gender identity seems. I could perhaps respect the sheer boldness of it if the execution hadn’t been so crappy AND if Audiard had found a way around the film’s central moral problem: the extraordinary generosity it extends to the lead character.

Let me recap. Karla Sofía Gascón plays Manitas, a drug cartel boss whose greatest wish is to transition in secret while faking his own death to escape this extremely violent and macho background. A few years after transitioning, now living happily as a Emilia Pérez; she contacts the lawyer played by Zoe Saldaña, who aided her at the beginning, to go back home.

Anyway, with the softer heart Emilia now possesses, she decides to try to make amends to the cartels’ victims and establishes an organization to help locate missing people. The movie frames this as wonderful work, but in the context of the real-world Mexico, we are talking about a staggering scale of cartel violence—the victims aren’t just people involved in drug trafficking, but also children, women, ordinary citizens—and thousands of families searching for missing relatives or just waiting for their remains to be found.

**And what’s being proposed here is that this fictional character who has VARIOUS real-life counterparts and would presumably have been responsible for hundreds (maybe thousands) of murders can suddenly escape her past and emerge happy, at peace with herself, with ALL the money accumulated through criminal activity—naturally, without answering for any of those crimes.** The suggestion, then, is that this attempt at making amends is enough.

At a certain point, Emilia allows her more violent self to resurface. (The movie, which also drew criticism from trans viewers, seems to treat her former identity as Manitas as a kind of “split personality.”) This final eruption of violence results in a tragedy from which Emilia emerges—wait for it!—sanctified. No, I’m not speaking figuratively. And that was all, the movie was over.

What did I even see? I don’t even know how to wrap this up except, I guess, by apologizing for reminding everyone that this film exists, and for ignoring the warnings of those who encouraged me and the world that it was not worth it.

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. It’s not really interested in the trans issue so much as the question of if one can escape from a violent past without actually taking accountability for their actions. Of course the answer is an obvious no, but it takes Emilia the whole movie to realize that, and they pay the price in the end.
2. This film feels like it was so heavily promoted like how a lot of Oscar bait films are:

It’s not about having a good film, but just making yourself look enlightened. And we all know how the Academy likes the idea of being progressive vs. actually being progressive.
3. I don’t see a meaningful difference between the cultural tourism of Emilia Perez vis-a-vis Mexico, and that of Dheepan vis-a-vis Tamils. They’re both pretty ludicrous melodramas, which isn’t to say that one isn’t allowed to enjoy watching them. Anyway, in short, I would’ve thought that if Emilia Perez could’ve worked for anyone, it would’ve been an Audiard fan. 

I liked his four films from Read My Lips to Rust and Bone really a lot, and found Dheepan to be a bit of a fall out of seriousness into superficiality and novelty cultural tourism.

Paris 13 Arrondissement was Audiard spinning his wheels with quasi soap opera material. Emilia Perez isn’t more serious than Dheepan, certainly, but I think it’s pretty good.
  - I hope one day Audiard does something that prompts a lot of people to reevaluate his career and specifically EP. To be clear, I don't think EP is a very good movie, I think its pretty annoying, the songs are just poorly written songs, and the musical set pieces are C- at best. I also don't think the movie should have ever been given the treatment it got in either direction. 

It became the awards season villain which put it in a certain framing. If people found it in a different way it's looked at so so differently. So many bad faith analyses looking at the lyrics to the vaginoplasty song not realizing how obviously intentional its being. No engaging in its reverence for the telenovela. I mean man, you see Read My Lips (a quite good film imo and a movie widely regarded as quite good), and you can 100% how he comes to make a goofy musical about sex, gender, cheating and guns
4. Check out *Johanne Sacreblu*, a parody short film by a Mexican queer artist, spoofing the surface-level stereotyping found in Emilia Perez by telling a similar-ish story occurring in a similarly cartoonish and overly simplified version of France
5. I'm a film school student in latam and one of my classes is Film Criticism, my professor for that class happens to be one of the biggest critics in the country (for whatever it's worth) and he has, on multiple ocassions, made it known that he actually quite likes Emilia Perez and that whoever doesn't is looking at it wrong. 

I don't share but respect most of his opinions, but this one has always left me dumbfounded

I'm not watching Emilia Perez, tho
6. I caught it late one night on Netflix and I made the happy mistake of watching the movie with the idea that Rita was the main character with Emilia as the antagonist that she had to endure. It struck me as a silly but dark comedy.  I was a bit befuddled when Rita disappeared for 15 minutes of the runtime  but was happy and re-engaged when she reappeared. It honestly never occurred to me that Emilia was meant to be the protagonist (despite the title) until Saldana was nominated for SA at the Oscars/the controversy erupted. 

 I enjoyed the movie in my own little odd and misguided bubble.  Apparently, being completely oblivious can be advantageous every now and then.



## 2. Various HiNTS of continuity/timelines in James Bond 007 movie franchise.

**Score:** 0
**Body:** **WARNING: Long Post (Summary in comment)**

Without any delay, straight to point, ofcourse you have to remember or rewatch the movies if YOU want to be sure. I won't try to establish a timeline but just lay it out there.😁

First, who is said popularly(but never ever officially, specially not with current meaning)a Re-boot.

**Craig Era:**

Then it cuts/jump to colored scenes, LeChiffre the villain with blood tears and parkour scene where 007 is experienced enough to get annoyed by a rookie touching his ears.

Then after getting out of hospital, there is some time spend with Vesper, then after the line "the bitch is dead" and James checking the phone, we see Mr White getting shot in leg. **SECOND** Skyfall 2012, takes place definatly after quite some time. It uses past/legacy and depends on it very hard. That is, to believe in the movie one have to know and have familiarity with character, as he is now a 'Old Dog'. We will cut of 'just nods/winks/homages' becasue there is limit to them, you have a object/car which is running and firing around becomes vital part of movie-in-universe. SO, whats there, Aston Martin with same number plate, M. knowing about the ejector seat(M, Q, Moneypenny have always been treated as regulars/stand-ins).

No its not the same car from Casino, THEN, Goldfinger, Thunderball have happened, there was a previous Q, old too, because 007 was surprised to see a young person and he says 'not exactly christmas', so he is used to high-gadgets. Without it all feels illegitimate, a movie have to have in-universe explaination, like Goldeneye opening scene of Aston drive, because they never deny it same guy.(They were trying to get same number plate in 1995 but legal problems).

So, craig's Bond have gone to Goldeneye, Thunderball, Goldeneye somehow-someway. As we see NTTD, we then know that he have even have The Living Daylights adventure.

If you notice, after Sam Mendes, there is so much emphasis on 'the world has changed, old ways etc.'. It all feels out of nowhere and without weight, if its not somehow, someway connected to previous movies.

OKAY, I won't enforce anything, I just put it out there what I saw as factual. That is they might have.

**Connery Era:**

What was the connection between Dr No and Russia With Love? A hidden organization's revenge. They were still more or less free. Goldfinger was completly free. Even Thunderball is standalone aside from the villain working. Bond is fighting them just from his side without much knowing about 'Spectre/Blofeld'. Until You Only Live Twice. Where he meets Blofeld for first time. You can't be sure how much time passes between each film.

**Then,** **Lazenby Era** On Her Majesty's Secret Service have another actor play the character, they thought that having their biggest villain yet is the best idea, and writers decided to lean on the book, making him meet here for first time, 'again'. So ONE/fan must overlook it, for his interests sake while making it as contextual as possible. Maybe one can RETCON and see that either he didn't see him face to face in YOLT or that YOLT takes place after OHMSS, and he meets again, but I will go with the previous option.

**Next**, Diamonds Are Forever, Bond is very eager to find Blofeld in the pre-title sequence. More angry and hard hitting. Ofcourse he can't kill someone out of personal vendetta. He in the end(of pre-title sequence of DAF) 'kills' Blofeld, his anger cools down and he moves on. Some time have probably past between that and main movie. Where Blofeld once more? make a absurd plan/revenge/ escape?-probably as he returns in FYEO. We will get to that.

**Moore Era:**

**So,** it starts with Live And Let Die, Bond is an expert and experienced agent here, as he seems to be at more ease and less taking things personally(not that he don't have personal feelings involved).

The Man With The Golden Gun, The Spy Who Loved Me, Moonraker, then For Your Eyes Only, here Bond have become experienced, and have made admirors/adversaries(Scarmanga etc.)

In FYEO, pre-title sequence we see, him standing infront of Tracy's grave, that prooves that event of OHMSS, somewhere. THEN octopussy, never say never again, a view to a kill, living daylights. (I will tell about NSNA and TLD later).

In Living Daylights, Bond feels more youthfull, doesn't he? then in Licence To Kill he is more mature, ofcourse he never a rookie. But definatly that. So in LTK its mentioned that he was infact married 'but that was long ago'. THEN

**Brosnan Era:**

Goldeneye film starts with pre-title sequence which takes place 9 YEARS before actual movie, where he iss accused of being a 'relic of certain war'. A dinasour. So that equal to being over-expert. Lot of experience.

**There** is no factual detial of when the next movies take place and how much gap is between each of them. I personally don't find him old or that-old looking in either Tomorrow Never Dies and The World Is Not Enough until Die Another Day. If I remeber correctl he have little white hairs. **Other** thing, Bond was re-evaluated in 1995 movie, while he was taken a job as trainer or retired and then called back and re-trained in Never Say Never Again, I know non-eon. but Fatima Blush😍

SO THAT IS THAT.

Now, you can see many timejumps and undefined gaps between movies, or in movies themselves. Again, if ONE chooses or get interested in making a as valid and profitable to ONE's personal desires of/from James Bond 007 movie franchise, he or she may, in this case like me see and choose:

**\[Spectre 2015, NttD 2021 are complete blunders, some of Skyfall too(like not saving Severine, making Moneypenny field agent, idiot of a Q, M dying), even QOS which I love, some part of it too(like not well executed and written,i.e. not bringing back formula and still whining about vesper.), OR any part of the movie which contridict what you want or probable continuity, can be cleared in portions, like he won't completly meet Blofeld in YOLT.\]**

This all could be cleared in as part of Fever Dream that Bond suffers in Die Another Day torture sequence, even that movie itself is seemingly 'over-the-top' becasue of Bond's unhealthy state.

**OKAY**, I would do this that is remove 2015 and 2021 movies almost completly and etc. than loose my liking of 'same old james bond'. That is I will treat CR2006 and QOS kind of prequels. LALD taking place between them as it was next novel after casino, along with TND, as it have have new kind of villain. Dr No is the first mission after 'that black and white scene and getting double o'.

TLD(youth feel) can take place after DN, same goes for FRWL, as it is immidiate spectre's revenge.

after quantum, movies like from Goldfinger, Goldeneye's Arkangel, Thunderball, YOLT, OHMSS, etc. could take place.

From TMWTGG, TSWLM, MR, FYEO(after OHMSS), TWINE, GE, AVTAK, LTK(after FYEO). SF(severine is saved, M don't die, just retires, q is not idiot, moneypenny is just desk worker).

Octopussy(Bond have been working long enough, that a 'victim' of his, daughter has became a danger),

NSNA after sometime.

There is lot of space where next james bond movie(s) could take place, they just have to follow the formula, make standalone-episodic, balance of campy and gritty. In first movie they can make joke about Moneypenny killing Bond, nightmare of having child and replaced, few refrences to past films, like dusty files of {skyfall, arkangel, dr no, moonraker, scanchez, thunderball etc.} and move on, with next movies simply being normal james bond movies.

**END**

Its fun to imagine its same Bond fighting and going through adventures of moonraker, living daylights, dr no, you only live twice, thunderball, live and let die, octopussy, the world is not enough, skyfall, quantum etc. Its a reason I like him, a kind of unsaid immortal feel, a forever friend. Different times and places.

Ofcourse one must know and accept that not one single James Bond movie actually follow any timeline/storyline/continuity, NO not even skyfall, quantum of solace, spectre, nttd, No not at all. Its just a FACT. Same goes for each actors.

One must take them as stories, and if interest there make a storyline by himself.

The title for next movie, my choice would be Nightfall.

2. The Bond franchise was created in an era that didn't suffer from the modern need for everything to be explained and connected. It used to be that heroes had continuing adventures, and there was very little connective tissue between them - other than the presence of the hero and his (usually always, "his") sidekicks, companions and rotating love interests. 

Connery, Lazenby, Moore, Dalton and Brosnan all ostensibly played the exact same character - the man who boiled Dr No to death is also the same man who fought an exo-skeletoned Elon Musk analogue over the skies of Korea while a space laser shot up the DMZ, and _everything_ in between.

There are nods and hints to past events here and there - Lazenby's "this didn't happen to the other guy" quip, references to Tracy in License to Kill, the racist redneck Sheriff in two Moore movies - but ultimately every Bond up to Casinao Royale is just another in "the continuing adventures of James Bond". That's why you can have four different actors play Blofeld, and why Blofeld in OHMSS doesn't remember Bond from You Only Live Twice. 

Craig plays a completely different version of Bond, separate from the first twenty films, and it's only in his films that rules of continuity are applied, because the franchise then becomes a series. Admittedly, the inclusion of the Aston Martin DB5 in Skyfall breaks the fourth wall quite heavily. The car is an anachronist nod to the previous Bond era that Craig was not a part of. 

Tl;dr - don't get too hung up on trying to force a throughline between every Bond movie. It's not worth it.

## 3. Which film is better, Fail Safe or Dr. Strangelove?

**Score:** 0
**Body:** Question, Which film is better, Fail Safe or Dr. Strangelove?

I re-watched Dr. Strangelove recently, and I have re-watched this film so many times. It truly is a great film, in large part because of the performances. Peter Sellers gives a master performance, George C. Scott gives a legendary performance, Slim Pickens, Sterling Hayden all great. What also made the film great is just how absurd the whole film is, and how Kubrick realized just how absurd the whole Nuclear Conflict is and how ludicrous it was for 2 mega-powers wo wipe us out for the pettiest and stupid reasons. Dr. Strangelove, to me, is a perfect, and probably one of Kubrick's Best.

On Fail Safe, I must admit, I only heard of this film because of Dr. Strangelove and how Kubrick & Peter George sued the production because they felt it infringed on Red Alert, the source material Dr. Strangelove was based on and managed to get the film released after Dr. Strangelove, this Fail Safe being overshadowed.

I heard people talk positively over the film, but I must admit, I haven't the film until just now, and I gotta say, It's a great film. While Dr. Strangelove is absurd, Fail Safe takes the whole premise seriously. Sidney Lumet masterfully directs the film, The performances are top notch, and I think the best performance was Henry Fonda.

I will say, You can tell the film was shot very cheaply. Granted, Dr. Strangelove was also shot cheap, but Fail Safe really looks like it wasn't made in the best conditions, and that Lumet had to shoot in own backyard. But I think it adds to the grittiness of the film.

Which is the better film, It's tough, but I'll give the edge to Dr. Strangelove. The Performances in Dr. Strangelove are just very memorable but I will admit, I was surprised with Fail Safe.

What do you think, Which film is better, Fail Safe or Dr. Strangelove?

## 4. Gone Girl (2014) - the last great Hollywood thriller?

**Score:** 0
**Body:** I remember this film being a real event. Based on a bestseller, Fincher directing, Affleck’s renaissance and a starring role for the mysterious Rosamund Pike.

And it didn’t disappoint. It felt like a truly high-end thriller. Clever, witty, dark, daring and with multiple twists and turns.

It’s 2.5 hours but feels like half that with the great pacing. I love that early scene when Det Rhonda Boney and her assistant are examining the house and asking Nick various questions. The police work is very satisfying and just how much do they suspect Nick? How much do \[i\]we\[/i\] suspect him? The film keeps your imagination so alive the whole time.

New awesome characters keep popping up - Tyler Perry as the ace lawyer, Sela Ward as the sympathetic talk-show host, Ratajkowksi as the student with the huge naturals, Doogie Howser as the creepy ex with a very memorable… fate. The guy who plays Amy’s previous victim is wonderfully sad and sympathetic. The gross trailer-trash couple who try to steal from Amy. Everyone *nails* their role.

The whole mood is delicious - Fincher’s sleek visuals and Reznor & Ross’ dreamy score combine to create a kind of perfect hell. You get totally lost in the film’s sexy macabre universe.

When was the last time you saw a top class Hollywood thriller with big stars and a decent budget. For me that was *twelve years ago* with Gone Girl.

I don’t understand why Fincher has been relegated to Netflix. He’s one of our greatest living directors and he should surely be cranking out more of these great thrillers - they’re awesome, everyone loves them, and they make bank 🤷🏻‍♂️
